title: Hangman Word Display
story: Game night! You're building Hangman for your friends. The player needs to see which letters they've guessed correctly and which remain hidden as underscores. That display — the core of the game — is one carefully crafted function.
why: Building a word display function teaches character-by-character string construction with conditional logic — each letter either reveals itself or stays hidden based on what's been guessed.
analogy: Hangman display is like a curtain covering a stage. Each guessed letter is a spotlight. When a spotlight hits a curtain panel (letter position), that panel drops to reveal the letter underneath. Unlit panels stay covered as underscores. The display function is the lighting technician — it checks each spotlight and each panel, deciding what the audience sees.
try_it: Add a `guess_letter(word: Str, guessed: Str, letter: Char) -> Str` function that adds a letter to the guessed string if it's not already there, then returns the updated display. Simulate a full game: start with "elephant" and guess 'e', 'a', 't', 'x' in sequence.
tips: Use a `found` flag: start false, set to true if any match occurs, then check the flag after the inner loop
The outer loop iterates the word; the inner loop checks the guessed string for a match
Build the result string with string.str_concat() one character at a time
An empty guessed string means no letters revealed — every position shows '_'
common_mistakes: Checking for exact string match instead of checking each guessed letter against each word letter
Forgetting to reset the `found` flag for each new character of the word
Using `=` instead of `==` inside the comparison condition
Returning inside the inner loop — you'd only process one character of the word
